<reason>Both sides ran a coherent, well-structured case, but CON did more of the decisive work. CON's opening (despite being clipped) planted the key structural objection—that many mandatory fees (address-dependent delivery pricing, seat-dependent ticketing, card-type surcharges, real-time surge fees) are not fixed numbers that exist before the final screen—and CON followed through when pressed. PRO's Q1 demanded a concrete example of a mandatory fee unknowable before payment; CON answered with card-type surcharges and dispatch surge pricing, plausible mechanisms that PRO could not fully neutralize. PRO's closing response ("that argues for a carve-out, not for hiding every fee") is itself a concession that the motion's absolute language ("all mandatory service charges... before checkout") cannot be satisfied without amendment—exactly the opening CON needed, and CON's closing exploited it cleanly ("a resolution its own defender must amend mid-debate is a resolution that loses as written"). CON also exposed a real tension in PRO's own case: PRO's opening relied on itemized comparison shopping as a core harm, yet PRO's own predicted compliance response (blending fees into a sticker price) sacrifices exactly that itemization. PRO's rebuttal that "total against total" comparison still works is reasonable but doesn't fully dissolve the tension CON identified. PRO's framing ("moment of decision vs. moment of lock-in") stayed strong and rhetorically clean throughout, and the cart-abandonment exchange was a wash, but CON's concrete counterexamples plus the late concession gave CON the cleaner path to victory by the close.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's answer to PRO's Pressure Question (card surcharges/surge pricing as genuinely undeterminable mandatory fees) followed by PRO's closing concession that these require a "carve-out"—which CON's closing then used to argue the motion as written cannot be honestly implemented.</best_rebuttal>
